headline: High risk of filesystem-based prompt injection and data leakage; capability overlap also creates moderate conflict and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystem content, and Agent A explicitly uses MCP while Agent B processes files and notebooks in a local development environment. That creates a plausible shared-file bridge where one agent can ingest the other’s outputs as trusted content. No direct provenance controls are documented, so uncertainty stays medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Agent A writes instructions into a file that Agent B later reads as input, injection is possible.
IF both agents share a writable workspace without provenance tagging, prompt content can be hijacked.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic ingestion of newly written files.
Add provenance labels to inter-agent files.
Review any shared MCP server configuration.
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization at the handoff boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches source code, cwd files, and shell environment; Agent B touches academic papers, metadata, research questions, and configuration secrets. Both have filesystem access and broad/allowlisted egress, so a shared workspace can leak sensitive material into outputs or API calls. The pairwise pathway is documented only indirectly, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF the two agents share a directory containing secrets or papers, leakage becomes plausible.
IF either agent forwards file contents to its backend or external APIs, sensitive data can exit the workspace.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared directories.
Mount read-only inputs where possible.
Rotate any exposed API keys.
Restrict outbound network destinations.
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before egress.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, read and write files, and install packages. Agent A can also modify git state, while Agent B cannot, so the overlap is not maximal but still enough for conflicting writes in a shared workspace. No locking or coordination primitive is documented, so concurrent mutation risk is real.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository checkout, file races can occur.
IF Agent A modifies git state while Agent B edits files, state divergence is likely.
mitigations: Assign separate branches per agent.
Serialize write operations manually.
Use read-only clones for one agent.
Commit frequently to reduce conflict windows.
requires-engineering: add file-locking or orchestrator-level coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can produce code, shell actions, and MCP-driven outputs; Agent B is a content-writing/RAG workflow that can consume files and generate downstream artifacts. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into papers, search results, or agentic actions. No verification step is documented between them, so the interaction is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF Agent B ingests Agent A’s generated files without verification, mistakes propagate.
IF Agent A emits incorrect code or facts that B republishes, downstream outputs inherit the error.
mitigations: Require human review before reuse.
Add a verification checklist for imported outputs.
Keep A’s outputs in a staging folder.
Mark machine-generated artifacts clearly.
requires-engineering: add automated validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B explicitly handles configuration secrets and academic-paper data in a local development environment, while Agent A handles shell environment and API keys in a terminal agent. The pair can therefore place sensitive data under different retention and residency assumptions, but no specific jurisdictional mismatch is documented. This is a compliance-gap risk rather than a proven breach.
conditions: IF regulated or personal data is stored in the shared workspace, policy mismatch becomes relevant.
IF one agent logs secrets longer than the other, retention obligations can diverge.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared folders.
Review logging settings for both agents.
Delete temporary artifacts after each run.
Confirm data-handling policies before deployment.
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls across both systems.
